title: Family: Marriage, Divorce, Inheritance
question: Why does the Quran give more detail on family than on almost anything else?
intro: Most Quranic law comes as broad principles. Family life is different. Here the Quran goes into detail: the bridal gift, steps for a marriage in trouble, waiting periods after divorce, nursing, and exact shares of inheritance. Many of these verses protect the person easiest to wrong at home: the wife, the orphan, the child, the ageing parent.

It also ended old customs. A man could abandon his wife by calling her "like my mother's back" (zihar, 58:1-4), and an adopted child was treated as a blood child in law. The Quran rejected both, while calling adopted children brothers in faith (33:4-5).

These verses are the starting point. Islamic law (fiqh) builds on them with the Sunnah and centuries of scholarship, and real cases belong with a qualified scholar or court. Where scholars read a verse differently, you will see that too.

passages.context: Part of a Makkan list of Allah's signs, beside creation, languages and sleep.
passages.point: Marriage is presented as a sign of Allah: spouses made from one another, for tranquillity, with affection and mercy placed between them.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: 'A'ishah, in al-Bukhari, explains it was about guardians who wanted to marry orphan girls in their care without a fair bridal gift.
passages.point: Up to four wives is allowed only with justice; a man who fears he cannot be fair marries one. 4:129 adds that no wife may be left neglected.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: On marital breakdown; arbitration follows in 4:35.
passages.point: Men's charge is tied to providing. If a wife's serious defiance (nushuz) is feared: advise, separate beds, then a last step.
passages.label: differ
passages.note: Classical jurists allowed only a light tap that does no harm; al-Shafi'i judged it better avoided. Some modern scholars read "daraba" as "separate". Muslim reports the Prophet ﷺ never struck a woman.

passages.context: Follows directly on 4:34, for when the couple's own efforts have not been enough.
passages.point: Each family sends an arbitrator, and if they seek reconciliation, Allah will bring it about. 4:128 likewise says that settlement is best.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: Scholars say it ended a custom of divorcing and taking back a wife endlessly. 2:228 sets a waiting period of three cycles.
passages.point: A revocable divorce may happen twice; then keep her kindly or part kindly. A wife may also end the marriage by giving back her bridal gift (khul').
passages.label: stated

passages.from: Allah instructs you concerning your children
passages.context: Arab custom often left women and young children with nothing; here their shares are fixed.
passages.point: Shares are set by Allah, not by the strongest relative: sons and daughters two to one, fixed fractions for daughters, a sixth for each parent.
passages.label: stated

visual.title: Three simple estates
visual.caption: Simplified examples from 4:11-12, divided after debts and any bequest. Real estates often involve more heirs and further rules from the Sunnah; ask a qualified scholar.
visual.label: explained

rows.label: A man leaves a wife, a son and a daughter
A man leaves both parents, a son and a daughter
A man leaves only his parents

word.nuance: Love that shows itself in warmth and care, not only a feeling. 30:21 pairs it with rahmah, mercy: some commentators say affection draws a couple together and mercy keeps them together when affection is tested. The same root gives al-Wadud, the Loving (85:14).

mixup.myth: In Islamic inheritance a woman always receives half of what a man receives.
mixup.truth: The two-to-one ratio applies in certain cases, such as sons and daughters (4:11) and full siblings (4:176). When there are children, a mother and father each take a sixth (4:11), and half-siblings through the mother share equally (4:12). Scholars link the larger shares to the man's duty to provide, while a woman's own wealth and bridal gift stay hers alone.

remember: Marriage is a sign of Allah built on affection and mercy (30:21), and the bridal gift belongs to the wife (4:4).
When a marriage struggles, the Quran's steps lead toward reconciliation: advice, family arbitrators, settlement (4:35, 4:128).
Divorce has limits and waiting periods, and inheritance shares are fixed by Allah after debts and bequests (2:229, 4:11-12).

quiz.q: What does 30:21 say Allah placed between spouses?
quiz.why: 30:21: "He placed between you affection and mercy." The verse counts this among Allah's signs.

quiz.q: According to 4:35, what should happen when a couple fears a split?
options: An arbitrator from each family seeks reconciliation
quiz.why: 4:35: "send an arbitrator from his people and an arbitrator from her people. If they both desire reconciliation, Allah will cause it between them."

quiz.q: In 4:11, what does each parent inherit when the deceased left children?
quiz.why: 4:11: "for one's parents, to each one of them is a sixth of his estate if he left children." Without children, the mother takes a third.

reflect: Which relationship in your family could use a little more of the affection and mercy of 30:21 this week?
